text:
The Nigerian Law School has denied allegations that female Muslim candidates wearing hijab were harassed or prevented from entering examination halls during the Bar Final Examinations held on October 31.
The school said it had no policy or institutional practice of religious discrimination, adding that its examination rules were designed to ensure proper identification, prevent malpractice and protect the integrity of examinations.
In a statement posted on its Facebook page on Wednesday, the Secretary to the Council and Director of Administration, Aderonke Osho, described the allegations as false.
The school disclosed that a female student wearing hijab was apprehended during the Bar Part I examinations on October 29 after she was allegedly found with an earpiece hidden in her hijab and a mobile phone strapped to her thigh.
It said the incident was still under investigation in line with its examination rules and relevant regulations.
The institution maintained that its security measures were applied fairly and without discrimination, citing Sections 38 and 42 of the Constitution, which guarantee freedom of religion and prohibit discrimination.
However, the Muslim Rights Concern (MURIC) has asked the Council of Legal Education to set up a probe panel to investigate the controversy.
In a statement on Thursday, its Executive Director, Professor Isiaq Akintola, said the council should immediately investigate the alleged restriction on hijab-wearing candidates.
He also called on the Director-General of the Law School to recuse herself to allow the panel to conduct a free, fair and transparent investigation.
MURIC condemned the alleged restriction, arguing that candidates should not suffer collective punishment over the alleged misconduct of an individual student.
Akintola further accused the Director-General of posing a threat to religious freedom and healthy interaction within the institution.
The organisation said the Nigerian Law School was governed by the Council of Legal Education and urged it to intervene without delay.
The Law School, meanwhile, urged the public to avoid premature conclusions and allow its investigation to establish the facts.
